Question: Can matter undergo continuous phase transitions?
Answer: Generally matter is always phase transitioning in both directions, at any temperature. For example, water even at room temperature will have molecules leaving the liquid state and joining the gaseous state, and other molecules leaving the gaseous state and joining the liquid state. It’s a matter of the rates. At room temperature, it’s much more likely for a molecule to transition from gas to liquid than from liquid to gas, so you wind up with “most” of your molecules in liquid form. There is always a partial pressure of water vapor present as well though. As you raise the temperature, you raise the chance of a liquid-to-gas transition and lower the chance of a gas-to-liqud transition, so the proportion of water in the liquid and gas states will adjust. At exactly the boiling point, the probability of a molecule transitioning is the same in either direction. So, these things are always happening. Stay safe and well! Question: What is the quantum field theory for someone just starting to learn it?
Answer: It’s a lot of math that’s fairly hard to learn, for one thing. Conceptually it’s not that awful - the basic process you go through is that you know what your “initial conditions” are (the particles you have coming in toward a potential interaction). You then basically guess at possible final configurations (particles created, annihilated, etc., and how they are behaving), and then you can calculate the probability of the initial config leading to that final config. You repeat this process for more guessed final configs, until the total probability you have accounted for so far gets close enough to 1.0 to suit you. If it’s well below 1.0, then there’s some final configuration you haven’t considered yet. That’s basically it. The math takes care of enforcing conservation laws and all other physical requirements. The big difference between this and classical physics is that you do not “calculate” the final configuration - you “propose it” (guess at it) and then see how likely that is. I assume that with experience you get better and knowing what final configs to consider. Stay safe and well! Question: Can you explain the concept of 'irreducible' representation and why particle states must be represented by them?
Answer: This is a loose analogy, but consider a ball rolling down a hill. Basically it tries to find its way to the lowest point it can. If there’s a little extra low spot at the bottom of the valley, and the ball has much of a chance of getting there, it will. What it’s basically “trying to do” is shed as much gravitational potential energy as it can - trying to reach the lowest energy state. Irreducible representations are like “breakdowns” of a math structure that can’t be broken down any further. They’re kind of like the extra low spots at the bottom of the hill. It’s not energy we’re talking about this time, but when we do physics we try to make models of what’s happening in the world and we try to make those models as simple as possible. We try to “remove as much complexity” as possible. Well, if we can express something in terms more simple than we’re doing so far, we will - we like that. So it’s “our desire for simplicity” rather than “minimizing energy,” but there’s still the same sort of tendency for the models to become expressed in simpler and simpler terms. As far as why these representations are irreducible, well, everything has some kind of limit on how simple it can be. Take a golf ball flying through the air. In general, to describe it we need to specify its x, y, and z locations, and its x, y, and z velocities or momenta. That’s six numbers, and it’s as simple as we can get it. There’s no way for us to use five numbers, or four, and still fully describe the golf ball. The mathematical structure of the situation just requires a certain amount of “descriptive freedom” in order to cover all the cases we need it to cover. I hope this makes sense. Stay safe and well! Question: Can you provide an intuitive explanation for how opening another closed door can increase your chances of winning in the "three-door problem"?
Answer: Sure. Initially you have three choices and no knowledge whatsoever of where the “good prize” is. So you clearly have one chance in three of choosing the right one. But now you gain new information. The host will open one of the other two doors. It will never be the door that has the “good prize” - he will show you either the “fair” prize or the “booby” prize. Then he offers you the opportunity to trade your first door, which has a one-in-three chance of hiding the good prize, for the remaining unopened door. But if you think about it for a minute, you will see that what he’s really offering you is the chance to trade your one door for both of the other doors. The fact that he’s opened one of them is irrelevant. After your initial choice, there is a 1/3 chance that your chosen door hides the good prize, and a 2/3 chance it’s behind one of the other two. He then rules out one of the other two, so that means that there is a 2/3 chance that it’s behind the one remaining door he offers you the chance to swap to. So, you should definitely swap - it doubles your chances of getting the good prize. Stay safe and well! Question: If J C Maxwell had not come up with his electro-magnetic equations in the 1860's is there anyone else who could have before 1900?
Answer: That is a very hard question to answer reliably. Work in electricity and magnetism had been ongoing for decades. Faraday, Ampere, etc. The experimental data was appearing, and the connection between electricity and magnetism was noticed - that all happened without Maxwell being necessary. In particular, Faraday’s work introduced the notion of fields that filled space to the study. What Maxwell brought to the table was a particularly mathematical mind. His whole project began with the goal of taking Faraday’s and Ampere’s work and placing it into a rigorous modern mathematical form. His training was right for this - he held the mathematical tools at his command. His work was almost straightforward, given his background. In the end, though, he looked at the result and recognized that it was flawed. There was a mathematical inconsistency in it, even after all of the known experimental phenomena had been properly inserted. Maxwell corrected this situation by adding a term to one of the equations. Here are Maxwell’s equations (in their modern form - Maxwell himself didn’t write them anything like this elegantly): In the last equation, Maxwell added the last term. It had never been noticed in earlier work because that factor 1/c^2 is a very, very small number. But the addition corrected the problems, and when Maxwell then studied those equations he recognized that propagating electromagnetic waves should exist. He calculated the speed they should propagate at, and recognized that value as the (already known) speed of light. This made him realize that light is simply a form of EM radiation, and that many other sorts of “light,” differing from visible light only by frequency, should exist. And that unlocked the door to radio, television, and all of the other applications of electromagnetic waves that form the basis of our technological culture today. It opened the way to a better understanding of issues plaguing ocean-floor telegraph cables, etc. Would someone else have done this by 1900? As I said, it’s very hard to say. I want to think “probably.” None of the steps Maxwell took were unimaginably inspired - they were things that you’d expect any properly competent (mathematically competent) person working in the field might have seen. So I think yes, but who knows? It might have taken decades longer. You should keep in mind that special relativity became necessary because Maxwell’s equations were fundamentally at odds with Newtonian mechanics. Everyone expected it would be Maxwell’s equations that “had to give,” but it wasn’t - when Einstein brought forth special relativity it was Newton’s mechanics that he modified. Also, the necessity for quantum mechanics arose out of the study of black body radiation, and Maxwell’s equations were necessary to make that necessity evident. So, if Maxwell’s equations had come later, a whole lot of other things would have come later too. Nuclear energy research would likely have been postponed, and World War II would have had an altogether different ending. So the alternative history you are asking about would have indeed been a very different one. Stay safe and well! Question: Is the fine-tuning of the multiverse necessary for its existence, or could it exist with different parameter values?
Answer: We don’t really know. The “fine tuning problem” is pretty much based on the idea that it could have more or less any set of values. And yet it has these values, which support “life like us.” So how did we get so lucky? That’s the fine tuning problem. If it turned out that there’s some really good reason that the parameters have to be more or less what they are, then the fine tuning problem goes away. The main problem is that we have only one example of a universe to study. So we really don’t know much about the possibility of other universes. Stay safe and well! Question: If we combine moving at such rapid speed through space, how close are we to reaching the speed of light?
Answer: It’s not possible to reach the speed of light. In high school you’re taught that kinetic energy of a moving mass is KE = m*v^2 / 2 However, this is only an approximate expression, valid when v is much less than the speed of light c. So, that’s valid for more or less everything you ever encounter, because those things move at a very small fraction of the speed of light. For example, the fastest a man-made object has ever moved is 430,000 mph (that was the Parker Solar Probe when it had spiraled in very close to the sun). But even that is only 0.064% of the speed of light, and the basic “inaccuracy” in the formula above goes as (v/c)^2, so the error factor associated with using the high school formula would be just 0.00064^2 = 0.0253 = 2.53%. The “correct at all speeds” formula for kinetic energy is KE = m*c^2*sqrt(1/(1-v^2/c^2) - 1] So, kinetic energy still goes up as you raise the speed of your mass. But no matter how much energy you invest in speeding up your object, it can never reach the speed of light - the kinetic energy tends toward infinity as the speed approaches the speed of light. So, it can never be done, and that is a theoretical conclusion - not a matter of “our technology is not good enough yet.” The theory allows us to get as close to the speed of light as we wish, but never all the way to that speed. Question: How does gravity warp space and what is the proof? Per GRT, gravity is a warping of spacetime - and we have verified that clocks move at different rates based on distance from 'gravity well' - hence warping of time. What is the proof of warped space?
Answer: You’re conflating the model with the world - the map with the territory. We have a mathematical apparatus which makes predictions about how our observations will turn out. That apparatus has reliably predicted many, many observations across a wide spectrum of situations. It predicts the correct orbit of Mercury, whereas Newton’s theory of gravity does not. It predicts the bending of light as it passes the eclipsed sun - exactly the right amount of bending - whereas Newton’s theory does not. And it predicts gravitational waves, which have now been detected. There are many more experiments and as far as I know the predictions have turned out correct every time. That is the “proof” - except it’s not actually proof . You don’t “prove” things in science - you prove things in math. In science you collect experimental data and look at how it either confirms or refutes a theory. General relativity has not been experimentally refuted, and it’s been confirmed many times. But tomorrow it could be refuted - that’s why we never say we’ve “proven” a scientific theory. Regarding the warping, that is just a way of interpreting the mathematics. We can’t actually observe spacetime. We only observe the things in spacetime, so we don’t have direct evidence as to what spacetime itself is doing. If you don’t like to think in terms of spacetime curvature, then don’t. You can still solve the equations and make predictions, and they’ll still be right. That is all there really is to it.
